entries.a644a3a22924857af17a5742f5f065ed58215578: <div sID="gen12212" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="96" osisID="Ps.96" sID="Ps.96"/> <div eID="gen12212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12213" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12214" type="x-p"/> This psalm is part of that which was delivered into the hand of Asaph and his brethren (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7">1 Chron. xvi. 7</reference>), by which it appears both that David was the penman of it and that it has reference to the bringing up of the ark to the city of David; whether that long psalm was made first, and this afterwards taken out of it, or this made first and afterwards borrowed to make up that, is not certain. But this is certain, that, though it was sung at the translation of the ark, it looks further, to the kingdom of Christ, and is designed to celebrate the glories of that kingdom, especially the accession of the Gentiles to it. Here is, I. A call given to all people to praise God, to worship him, and give glory to him, as a great and glorious God, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. Notice given to all people of God's universal government and judgment, which ought to be the matter of universal joy, <reference osisRef="Ps.10">ver. 10-13</reference>. In singing this psalm we ought to have our hearts filed with great and high thoughts of the glory of God and the grace of the gospel, and with an entire satisfaction in Christ's sovereign dominion and in the expectation of the judgment to come.
entries.8a4961575ff16c342e821b0bac5f3026af373e1a: <div eID="gen12214" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12213" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Invitation to Praise and Honour God; A Call to Glorify God.</title> <div sID="gen12215" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> a new song: sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all the earth. <hi type="super">2</hi> Sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , bless his name; show forth his salvation from day to day. <hi type="super">3</hi> Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> great, and greatly to be praised: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> to be feared above all gods. <hi type="super">5</hi> For all the gods of the nations <hi type="italic">are</hi> idols: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made the heavens. <hi type="super">6</hi> Honour and majesty <hi type="italic">are</hi> before him: strength and beauty <hi type="italic">are</hi> in his sanctuary. <hi type="super">7</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O ye kindreds of the people, give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> glory and strength. <hi type="super">8</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the glory <hi type="italic">due unto</hi> his name: bring an offering, and come into his courts. 9 O worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth. <div eID="gen12215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12216" type="x-p"/> These verses will be best expounded by pious and devout affections working in our souls towards God, with a high veneration for his majesty and transcendent excellency. The call here given us to praise God is very lively, the expressions are raised and repeated, to all which the echo of a thankful heart should make agreeable returns. <div eID="gen12216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12217" type="x-p"/> I. We are here required to honour God, <div eID="gen12217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12218" type="x-p"/> 1. With songs, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Three times we are here called to <hi type="italic">sing unto the Lord;</hi> sing to the Father, to the Son, to the Holy Ghost, as it was <hi type="italic">in the beginning,</hi> when <hi type="italic">the morning stars sang together, is now,</hi> in the church militant, and <hi type="italic">ever shall be,</hi> in the church triumphant. We have reason to do it often, and we have need to be often reminded of it, and stirred up to it. <hi type="italic">Sing unto the Lord,</hi> that is, "<hi type="italic">Bless his name,</hi> speak well of him, that you may bring others to think well of him." (1.) <hi type="italic">Sing a new song,</hi> an excellent song, the product of new affections, clothed with new expressions. We speak of nothing more despicable than "an old song," but the newness of a song recommends it; for there we expect something surprising. A new song is a song for new favours, for those compassions which are new every morning. A new song is New-Testament song, a song of praise for the new covenant and the precious privileges of that covenant. A new song is a song that shall be ever new, and shall never wax old nor vanish away; it is an everlasting song, that shall never be antiquated or out of date. (2.) Let all the earth sing this song, not the Jews only, to whom hitherto the service of God had been appropriated, who could not <hi type="italic">sing the Lord's song in</hi> (would not sing it to) <hi type="italic">a strange land;</hi> but let <hi type="italic">all the earth,</hi> all that are <hi type="italic">redeemed from the earth, learn</hi> and sing <hi type="italic">this new song,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.3">Rev. xiv. 3</reference>. This is a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles; all the earth shall have this <hi type="italic">new song put into their mouths,</hi> shall have both cause and call to sing it. (3.) Let the subject-matter of this song be <hi type="italic">his salvation,</hi> the great salvation which was to be wrought out by the Lord Jesus; that must be shown forth as the cause of this joy and praise. (4.) Let this song be sung constantly, not only in the times appointed for the solemn feasts, but from day to day; it is a subject that can never be exhausted. Let day unto day utter this speech, that, under the influence of gospel devotions, we may daily exemplify a gospel conversation. <div eID="gen12218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12219" type="x-p"/> 2. With sermons (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Declare his glory among the heathen,</hi> even <hi type="italic">his wonders among all people.</hi> (1.) Salvation by Christ is here spoken of as a work of wonder, and that in which the glory of God shines very brightly; in showing forth that salvation we declare God's glory as it shines in the face of Christ. (2.) This salvation was, in the Old-Testament times, as heaven's happiness is now, <hi type="italic">a glory to be revealed;</hi> but in the fulness of time it was declared, and a full discovery made of that, even to babes, which prophets and kings desired and wished to see and might not. (3.) What was then discovered was declared only among the Jews, but it is now declared <hi type="italic">among the heathen, among all people;</hi> the nations which long sat in darkness now see this great light. The apostles' commission to preach the gospel to every creature is copied from this: <hi type="italic">Declare his glory among the heathen.</hi> <div eID="gen12219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12220" type="x-p"/> 3. With religious services, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.7-Ps.96.9">v. 7-9</reference>. Hitherto, though in every nation those that feared God and wrought righteousness were accepted of him, yet instituted ordinances were the peculiarities of the Jewish religion; but, in gospel-times, the kindreds of the people shall be invited and admitted into the service of God and be as welcome as ever the Jews were. The court of the Gentiles shall no longer be an outward court, but shall be laid in common with the court of Israel. All the earth is here summoned to fear before the Lord, to worship him according to his appointment. <hi type="italic">In every place incense shall be offered to his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.17">Zech. xiv. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Isa. lxvi. 23</reference>. This indeed spoke mortification to the Jews, but, withal, it gave a prospect of that which would redound very much to the glory of God and to the happiness of mankind. Now observe how the acts of devotion to God are here described. (1.) We must <hi type="italic">give unto the Lord;</hi> not as if God needed any thing, or could receive any thing, from us or any creature, which was not his own before, much less be benefited by it; but we must in our best affections, adorations, and services, return to him what we have received from him, and do it freely, as what we give; for <hi type="italic">God loves a cheerful giver.</hi> It is debt, it is rent, it is tribute, it is what must be paid, and, if not, will be recovered, and yet, if it come from holy love, God is pleased to accept it as a gift. (2.) We must acknowledge God to be the sovereign Lord and pay homage to him accordingly (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give unto the Lord glory and strength, glory and empire,</hi> or <hi type="italic">dominion,</hi> so some. As a king, he is clothed with robes of glory and girt with the girdle of power, and we must subscribe to both. <hi type="italic">Thine is the kingdom,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">thine is the power and the glory.</hi> "Give the glory to God; do not take it to yourselves, nor give it to any creature." (3.) We must <hi type="italic">give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name,</hi> that is, to the discovery he has been pleased to make of himself to the children of men. In all the acts of religious worship this is that which we must aim at, to honour God, to pay him some of that reverence which we owe him as the best of beings and the fountain of our being. (4.) We must <hi type="italic">bring an offering in to his courts.</hi> We must bring ourselves, in the first place, the <hi type="italic">offering up of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom. xv. 16</reference>. We must offer up the <hi type="italic">sacrifices of praise continually</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), must often appear before God in public worship and never appear before him empty. (5.) We must <hi type="italic">worship him in the beauty of holiness,</hi> in the solemn assembly where divine institutions are religiously observed, the beauty of which is their holiness, that is, their conformity to the rule. We must worship him with holy hearts, sanctified by the grace of God, devoted to the glory of God, and purified from the pollutions of sin. (6.) We must <hi type="italic">fear before him;</hi> all the acts of worship must be performed from a principle of the fear of God and with a holy awe and reverence. <div eID="gen12220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12221" type="x-p"/> II. In the midst of these calls to praise God and give glory to him glorious things are here said of him, both as motives to praise and matter of praise: <hi type="italic">The Lord is great, and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">greatly to be praised</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">v. 4</reference>) and <hi type="italic">to be feared,</hi> great and honourable to his attendants, great and terrible to his adversaries. Even the new song proclaims God great as well as good; for his goodness is his glory; and, when the everlasting gospel is preached, it is this, <hi type="italic">Fear God, and give glory to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 6, 7</reference>. 1. He is great in his sovereignty over all that pretend to be deities; none dare vie with him: <hi type="italic">He is to be feared above all gods</hi>—all princes, who were often deified after their deaths, and even while they lived were adored as petty gods—or rather all idols, <hi type="italic">the gods of the nations</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.96.5">v. 5</reference>. All the earth being called to sing the new song, they must be convinced that the Lord Jehovah, to whose honour they must sing it, is the one only living and true God, infinitely above all rivals and pretenders; he is great, and they are little; he is all, and they are <hi type="italic">nothing;</hi> so the word used for idols signifies, for we know that <hi type="italic">an idol is nothing in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1 Cor. viii. 4</reference>. 2. He is great in his right, even to the noblest part of the creation; for it is his own work and derives its being from him: <hi type="italic">The Lord made the heavens</hi> and all their hosts; they <hi type="italic">are the work of his fingers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.3">Ps. viii. 3</reference>), so nicely, so curiously, are they made. The gods of the nations were all made—gods, the creatures of men's fancies; but our God is the Creator of the sun, moon, and stars, those lights of heaven, which they imagined to be gods and worshipped as such. 3. He is great in the manifestation of his glory both in the upper and lower world, among his angels in heaven and his saints on earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Splendour and majesty are before him,</hi> in his immediate presence above, where the angels cover their faces, as unable to bear the dazzling lustre of his glory. <hi type="italic">Strength and beauty are in his sanctuary,</hi> both that above and this below. In God there is every thing that is awful and yet every thing that is amiable. If we attend him in his sanctuary, we shall behold his beauty, for <hi type="italic">God is love,</hi> and experience his strength, for <hi type="italic">he is our rock.</hi> Let us therefore go forth in his strength, enamoured with his beauty.
entries.6b6f17888a8275fb39e87fe3f33459656c1cd5e7: <div eID="gen12221" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Kingdom of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen12222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Say among the heathen <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved: he shall judge the people righteously. <hi type="super">11</hi> Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. <hi type="super">12</hi> Let the field be joyful, and all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice <hi type="super">13</hi> Before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth. <div eID="gen12222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12223" type="x-p"/> We have here instructions given to those who were to preach the gospel to the nations what to preach, or to those who had themselves received the gospel what account to give of it to their neighbours, what to <hi type="italic">say among the heathen;</hi> and it is an illustrious prophecy of the setting up of the kingdom of Christ upon the ruins of the devil's kingdom, which began immediately after his ascension and will continue in the doing till the mystery of God be finished. <div eID="gen12223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12224" type="x-p"/> I. Let it be told <hi type="italic">that the Lord reigns,</hi> the Lord Christ reigns, that King whom God determined to set upon his holy hill of Zion. See how this was first said <hi type="italic">among the heathen</hi> by Peter, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.42">Acts x. 42</reference>. Some of the ancients added a gloss to this, which by degrees crept into the text, <hi type="italic">The Lord reigneth from the tree</hi> (so Justin Martyr, Austin, and others, quote it), meaning the cross, when he had this title written over him, <hi type="italic">The King of the Jews.</hi> It was because he became obedient to death, even the death of the cross, that God exalted him, and gave him a name above every name, a throne above every throne. Some of the heathen came betimes to enquire after him that was <hi type="italic">born King of the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.2.2">Matt. ii. 2</reference>. Now let them know that he has come and his kingdom is set up. <div eID="gen12224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12225" type="x-p"/> II. Let it be told that Christ's government will be the world's happy settlement. <hi type="italic">The world also shall be established, that it shall not be moved.</hi> The natural world shall be established. The standing of the world, and its stability, are owing to the mediation of Christ. Sin had given it a shock, and still threatens it; but Christ, as Redeemer, upholds all things, and preserves the course of nature. The world of mankind shall be established, shall be preserved, till all that belong to the election of grace are called in, though a guilty provoking world. The Christian religion, as far as it is embraced, shall establish states and kingdoms, and preserve good order among men. The church in the world shall be established (so some), that it <hi type="italic">cannot be moved; for it is built upon a rock, and the gates of hell shall never prevail against it;</hi> it is a <hi type="italic">kingdom that cannot be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen12225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12226" type="x-p"/> III. Let them be told that Christ's government will be incontestably just and righteous: <hi type="italic">He shall judge the people righteously</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">judge the world with righteousness, and with his truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">v. 13</reference>. Judging is here put for ruling; and though this may be extended to the general judgment of the world at the last day, which will be <hi type="italic">in righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>), yet it refers more immediately to Christ's first coming, and the setting up of his kingdom in the world by the gospel. He says himself, <hi type="italic">For judgment have I come into this world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">John ix. 39</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.31">xii. 31</reference>), and declares that <hi type="italic">all judgment was committed to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22">John v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. His ruling and judging with righteousness and truth signify, 1. That all the laws and ordinances of his kingdom shall be consonant to the rules and principles of eternal truth and equity, that is, to the rectitude and purity of the divine nature and will. 2. That all his administrations of government shall be just and faithful, and according to what he has said. 3. That he shall rule in the hearts and consciences of men by the commanding power of truth and the Spirit of righteousness and sanctification. When Pilate asked our Saviour, <hi type="italic">Art thou a king?</hi> he answered, <hi type="italic">For this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.18.37">John xviii. 37</reference>); for he rules by truth, commands men's wills by informing their judgments aright. <div eID="gen12226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12227" type="x-p"/> IV. Let them be told that his coming draws nigh, that this King, this Judge, <hi type="italic">standeth before the door; for he cometh, for he cometh.</hi> Enoch, the seventh from Adam, said so. <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord cometh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>. Between this and his first coming the revolutions of many ages intervened, and yet he came at the set time, and so sure will his second coming be; though it is now long since it was said, <hi type="italic">Behold, he comes in the clouds</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>) and he has not yet come. See <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 4</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen12227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12228" type="x-p"/> V. Let them be called upon to rejoice in this honour that is put upon the Messiah, and this great trust that is to be lodged in his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.11-Ps.96.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let heaven and earth rejoice, the sea, the field,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all the trees of the wood.</hi> The dialect here is poetical; the meaning is, 1. That the days of the Messiah will be joyful days, and, as far as his grace and government are submitted to, will bring joy along with them. We have reason to give that place, that soul, joy into which Christ is admitted. See an instance of both, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.4-Acts.8.25 Acts.8.26-Acts.8.40">Acts viii.</reference> When Samaria received the gospel <hi type="italic">there was great joy in that city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.8">v. 8</reference>), and, when the eunuch was baptized, <hi type="italic">he went on his way rejoicing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">v. 39</reference>. 2. That it is the duty of every one of us to bid Christ and his kingdom welcome; for, though he comes conquering and to conquer, yet he comes peaceably. <hi type="italic">Hosanna, Blessed is he that cometh;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Hosanna, Blessed be the kingdom of our father David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.9-Mark.11.10">Mark xi. 9, 10</reference>); not only <hi type="italic">let the daughter of Zion rejoice that her King comes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>), but let all rejoice. 3. That the whole creation will have reason to rejoice in the setting up of Christ's kingdom, even <hi type="italic">the sea</hi> and <hi type="italic">the field;</hi> for, as by the sin of the first Adam the whole creation was made <hi type="italic">subject to vanity,</hi> so by the grace of the second Adam it shall, some way or other, first or last, be <hi type="italic">delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20-Rom.8.21">Rom. viii. 20, 21</reference>. 4. That there will, in the first place, be <hi type="italic">joy in heaven, joy in the presence of the angels of God;</hi> for, when the First-begotten was brought into the world, they sang their anthems to his praise, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Luke ii. 14</reference>. 5. That God will graciously accept the holy joy and praises of all the hearty well-wishers to the kingdom of Christ, be their capacity ever so mean. <hi type="italic">The sea</hi> can but <hi type="italic">roar,</hi> and how <hi type="italic">the trees of the wood</hi> can show that they <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> I know not; but <hi type="italic">he that searches the heart knows what is the mind of the Spirit,</hi> and understands the language, the broken language, of the weakest.  <chapter eID="Ps.96"/> <div eID="gen12228" type="x-p"/>

entries.ffb89e793d5b14ba7efbf80d1db0c026cc7c5d32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6616"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 96</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference>. The substance of this Psalm, and portions of the ninety-seventh, ninety-eighth, and hundredth, are found in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:7-36</reference>, which was used by David's directions in the dedication of the tabernacle on Mount Zion. The dispensation of the Messiah was typified by that event, involving, as it did, a more permanent seat of worship, and the introduction of additional and more spiritual services. Hence the language of these Psalms may be regarded as having a higher import than that pertinent to the occasion on which it was thus publicly used.</title> <div sID="gen10133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6616"/>1-3. All nations are invited to unite in this most joyful praise.<div eID="gen10133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new song--</hi>literally, "fresh," or new mercies (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.3">Psa 33:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.3">40:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10134" type="x-p"/>
entries.139d36a54b2a5ee4b44457cb4e3e6b8cc46feb3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6618"/><div sID="gen10137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6618"/>4-5. For He is not a local God, but of universal agency, while idols are nothing. <div eID="gen10137" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cc653abad7177c24406162d203e9c833a4a4aeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6619"/><div sID="gen10138" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6619"/><hi type="bold">6. Honour and majesty--</hi>are His attendants, declared in His mighty works, while power and grace are specially seen in His spiritual relations to His people. <div eID="gen10138" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ea9e26f366bc4033ca9f6d596605dee14a4f98a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6620"/><div sID="gen10139" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6620"/><hi type="bold">7-9. Give--</hi>or, "ascribe" (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>) due honor to Him, by acts of appointed and solemn worship in His house. <div eID="gen10139" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c3305a17610ef2d6f3f862f0b01e5e052431d90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6623"/><div sID="gen10143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6623"/>10. Let all know that the government of the world is ordered in justice, and they shall enjoy firm and lasting peace (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.3">Psa 72:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen10143" type="x-p"/>
entries.db65e1994db85409f49a63f639a0c6bb9ebdf025: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6624"/><div sID="gen10144" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6624"/>11-13. For which reason the universe is invoked to unite in joy, and even inanimate nature (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.14-Rom.8.22">Ro 8:14-22</reference>) is poetically represented as capable of joining in the anthem of praise. <chapter eID="Ps.96"/>

entries.fedfa706d6bb483fc537dce86fdbb3b0ee411426: <div eID="gen21795" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21798" type="x-p"/> All the inhabitants of the earth are invited to praise the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.1-Psa.96.3">Psa 96:1-3</reference>. His supreme majesty, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.3-Psa.96.6">Psa 96:3-6</reference>. The tribes of Israel are invited to glorify him, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.7-Psa.96.9">Psa 96:7-9</reference>; and to proclaim him among the heathen, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference>. The heavens and the earth are commamded to rejoice in him, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.11-Psa.96.13">Psa 96:11-13</reference>. <div eID="gen21798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21799" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title, either in the Hebrew or Chaldee. The Syriac: "Of David. A prophecy of the advent of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles to believe in him." The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic have, "A Song of David, when the House was built after the Captivity." We have seen in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.33">1Chr 16:23-33</reference> (note) a Psalm nearly like this, composed by David, on bringing the ark to Sion, from the house of Obed-edom. See the notes on the above place. But the Psalm, as it stands in the Chronicles, has thirty verses; and this is only a section of it, from the twenty-third to the thirty-third. It is very likely that this part was taken from the Psalm above mentioned, to be used at the dedication of the second temple. The one hundred and fifth Psalm is almost the same as that in Chronicles, but much more extensive. Where they are in the main the same, there are differences for which it is not easy to account. <div eID="gen21799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21800" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21801" type="x-p"/> Sing unto the Lord a new song - A song of peculiar excellence, for in this sense the term new is repeatedly taken in the Scriptures. He has done extraordinary things for us, and we should excel in praise and thanksgiving.
entries.3bc80c984c810c3f377c905d804a730e538cc1e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21802" type="x-p"/> Show forth his salvation from day to day - The original is very emphatic, בשרו מיום ליום ישועתו basseru miyom leyom yeshuatho "Preach the Gospel of his salvation from day to day." To the same effect the Septuagint, Ευαγγελιζεσθε ἡμεραν εξ ἡμερας το σωτηριον αυτου, "Evangelize his salvation from day to day."
entries.71ba15448da10105666b26971f21c61742ce22a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21803" type="x-p"/> Declare his glory among the heathen - The heathen do not know the true God: as his being and attributes are at the foundation of all religion, these are the first subjects of instruction for the Gentile world. Declare, ספרו sapperu, detail, number out his glory, כבודו kebodo, his splendor and excellence. <div eID="gen21803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21804" type="x-p"/> His wonders among all people - Declare also to the Jews his wonders, נפלאותיו niphleothaiv, his miracles. Dwell on the works which he shall perform in Judea. The miracles which Christ wrought among the Jews were full proof that he was not only the Messiah, but the mighty power of God.
entries.24e7b0750eccd526b59a5b20206e9f3be33e6160: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21805" type="x-p"/> He is to be feared above all gods - I think the two clauses of this verse should be read thus: - <div eID="gen21805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21806" type="x-p"/> Jehovah is great, and greatly to be praised. <div eID="gen21806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21807" type="x-p"/> Elohim is to be feared above all. <div eID="gen21807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21808" type="x-p"/> I doubt whether the word אלהים Elohim is ever, by fair construction, applied to false gods or idols. The contracted form in the following verse appears to have this meaning.
entries.7cdce6325e7eb6052992a86fdcb386ea1a52f3e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21809" type="x-p"/> All the gods of the nations are idols - אלהי elohey. All those reputed or worshipped as gods among the heathens are אלילים elilim, vanities, emptinesses, things of nought. Instead of being Elohim, they are elilim; they are not only not God, but they are nothing." "Jehovah made the heavens." He who is the creator is alone worthy of adoration.
entries.d592a2dca8197e283d43e6db5bd837e384e75053: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> Honour and majesty are before him - Does this refer to the cloud of his glory that preceded the ark in their journeying through the wilderness? The words strength and beauty, and glory and strength, <reference osisRef="Psa.96.7">Psa 96:7</reference>, are those by which the ark is described, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.61">Psa 78:61</reference>.
entries.4dce17ded6b98a07a2554bf5950efee6ef1dc5d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21811" type="x-p"/> Ye kindreds of the people - Ye families, all the tribes of Israel in your respective divisions.
entries.252406f449b5c338f48eebfcdfde1e0f18e99f43: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21812" type="x-p"/> Come into his courts - Probably referring to the second temple. The reference must be either to the tabernacle or temple.
entries.cdd1d18bddd3b2b8df74755bc45025155c7f0839: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21813" type="x-p"/> Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness - I think בהדרת קדש behadrath kodesh, signifies holy ornaments, such as the high priest wore in his ministrations. These were given him for glory and beauty; and the psalmist calls on him to put on his sacerdotal garments, to bring his offering, מנחה minchah, and come into the courts of the Lord, and perform his functions, and make intercession for the people.
entries.3f98e16eeda498506ea123b8817b63b9d6335eb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21814" type="x-p"/> Say among the heathen that the Lord reigneth - Justin Martyr, in his dialogue with Trypho the Jew, quotes this passage thus: Ειπατε εν τοις εθνεσι, ὁ Κυριος εβασιλευσε απο του ξυλου, "Say among the nations, the Lord ruleth by the wood," meaning the cross; and accuses the Jews of having blotted this word out of their Bibles, because of the evidence it gave of the truth of Christianity. It appears that this reading did exist anciently in the Septuagint, or at least in some ancient copies of that work, for the reading has been quoted by Tertullian, Lactantius, Arnobius, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Pope Leo, Gregory of Tours, and others. The reading is still extant in the ancient Roman Psalter, Dominus regnavit a ligno, and in some others. In an ancient MS. copy of the Psalter before me, while the text exhibits the commonly received reading, the margin has the following gloss: Regnavit a ligno crucis, "The Lord reigns by the wood of the cross." My old Scotico - Latin Psalter has not a ligno in the text, but seems to refer to it in the paraphrase: For Criste regned efter the dede on the crosse. It is necessary, however, to add, that no such words exist in any copy of the Hebrew text now extant, nor in any MS. yet collated, nor in any of the ancient Versions. Neither Eusebius nor Jerome even refer to it, who wrote comments on the Psalms; nor is it mentioned by any Greek writer except Justin Martyr. <div eID="gen21814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21815" type="x-p"/> The world also shall be established - The word תבל tebel signifies the habitable globe, and may be a metonymy here, the container put for the contained. And many think that by it the Church is intended; as the Lord, who is announced to the heathen as reigning, is understood to be Jesus Christ; and his judging among the people, his establishing the holy Gospel among them, and governing the nations by its laws.
entries.8fe6e269a9c31965122142ca8698865bff2dac50: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21816" type="x-p"/> Let the heavens rejoice - The publication of the Gospel is here represented as a universal blessing; the heavens the earth, the sea, and its inhabitants, the field, the grass, and the trees of the wood, are all called to rejoice at this glorious event. This verse is well and harmoniously translated in the old Psalter: - <div eID="gen21816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21817" type="x-p"/> Fayne be hevenes - and the erth glad; <div eID="gen21817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21818" type="x-p"/> Styrde be the see, - and the fulnes of it; <div eID="gen21818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21819" type="x-p"/> Joy sal feldes, - and al that ere in thaim. <div eID="gen21819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21820" type="x-p"/> And the paraphrase is at least curious: - <div eID="gen21820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21821" type="x-p"/> Hevens, haly men. Erthe, meke men that receyves lare (learning). Feldes, that is even men, mylde and softe: they shall joy in Criste. And all that is in thaim, that es, strengh, wyttes &skill." <div eID="gen21821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21822" type="x-p"/> I shall give the remaining part of this ancient paraphrase, which is an echo of the opinion of most of the Latin fathers. <reference osisRef="Psa.96.12">Psa 96:12</reference> Thou sal glad al the trese of woddes - Thou, that is in another Iyfe. Trese of woddes. - Synful men that were fyrst withouten frut, and sithen taken into God's temple. <reference osisRef="Psa.96.13">Psa 96:13</reference>. For he coms, he coms. He coms, fyrste to be man - Sythen he comes to deme the erth. <div eID="gen21822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21823" type="x-p"/> He sal deme in ebenes the erth: - and folk in his sothfastnes. Nothing is evener, or sothfaster, than that he geder with hym perfyte men; to deme and to deperte to the rig hande (thaim) that did mercy: - pase to the lefte hande (thaim) that did it nogt. <div eID="gen21823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21824" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here in the true spirit of poetry, gives life and intelligence to universal nature, producing them all as exulting in the reign of the Messiah, and the happiness which should take place in the earth when the Gospel should be universally preached. These predictions seem to be on the eve of complete fulfillment. Lord, hasten the time! For a fuller explanation see the following analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.96"/> <div eID="gen21824" type="x-p"/>

entries.5cf457f9613e93bbd2ed52dde6e80eca019711ed: <div eID="gen9941" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">A Greeting of the Coming Kingdom of God</title> <div sID="gen9942" type="x-p"/> What <reference osisRef="Ps.95.3">Psa 95:3</reference> says: <hi type="italic">“A great God is Jahve, and a great King above all gods,”</hi> is repeated in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference>-13. The lxx inscribes it (1) ᾠδὴ τῷ Δαυίδ, and the chronicler has really taken it up almost entire in the song which was sung on the day when the Ark was brought in (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:23-33</reference>); but, as the coarse seams between vv. 22-23, vv. 33-34 show, he there strings together familiar reminiscences of the Psalms (vid., on Ps 105) as a sort of mosaic, in order approximately to express the festive mood and festive strains of that day. And (2) ὅτε ὁ οἶκος ᾠκοδομεῖτο (Cod. Vat. ᾠκοδόμηται) μετὰ τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν. By this the lxx correctly interprets the Psalm as a post-exilic song: and the Psalm corresponds throughout to the advance which the mind of Israel has experienced in the Exile concerning its mission in the world. The fact that the religion of Jahve is destined for mankind at large, here receives the most triumphantly joyous, lyrical expression. And so far as this is concerned, the key-note of the Psalm is even deutero-Isaianic. For it is one chief aim of <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> to declare the pinnacle of glory of the Messianic apostolic mission on to which Israel is being raised through the depth of affliction of the Exile. All these post-exilic songs come much nearer to the spirit of the New Testament than the pre-exilic; for the New Testament, which is the intrinsic character of the Old Testament freed from its barriers and limitations, is in process of coming into being (<hi type="italic">im Werden begriffen</hi>) throughout the Old Testament, and the Exile was one of the most important crises in this progressive process. <div eID="gen9942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9943" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference> are more Messianic than many in the strict sense of the word Messianic; for the central (gravitating) point of the Old Testament gospel (<hi type="italic">Heilsverkündigung</hi>) lies not in the Messiah, but in the appearing (parusia) of Jahve - a fact which is explained by the circumstance that the mystery of the incarnation still lies beyond the Old Testament knowledge or perception of salvation. All human intervention in the matter of salvation accordingly appears as purely human, and still more, it preserves a national and therefore outward and natural impress by virtue of the national limit within which the revelation of salvation has entered. If the ideal Davidic king who is expected even does anything superhuman, he is nevertheless only a man - a man of God, it is true, without his equal, but not the God-man. The mystery of the incarnation does, it is true, the nearer it comes to actual revelation, cast rays of its dawning upon prophecy, but the sun itself remains below the horizon: redemption is looked for as Jahve’s own act, and “Jahve cometh” is also still the watchword of the last prophet (Mal 3:1). <div eID="gen9943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9944" type="x-p"/> The five six-line strophes of the Psalm before us are not to be mistaken. The chronicler has done away with five lines, and thereby disorganized the strophic structure; and one line (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference></hi>) he has removed from its position. The originality of the Psalm in the Psalter, too, is revealed thereby, and the non-independence of the chronicler, who treats the Psalm as an historian.
entries.6db27515d4d2a23d0bec19754163e2613005119c: <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3">Psa 96:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9945" type="x-p"/> Call to the nation of Jahve to sing praise to its God and to evangelize the heathen. שׁירוּ is repeated three times. The new song assumes a new form of things, and the call thereto, a present which appeared to be a beginning that furnished a guarantee of this new state of things, a beginning viz., of the recognition of Jahve throughout the whole world of nations, and of His accession to the lordship over the whole earth. The new song is an echo of the approaching revelation of salvation and of glory, and this is also the inexhaustible material of the joyful tidings that go forth from day to day (מיּום ליום as in <reference osisRef="Esth.3.7">Est 3:7</reference>, whereas in the Chronicles it is מיום אל־יום as in Num 30:15). We read <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference></hi> verbally the same in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.10">Isa 42:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.2">Psa 96:2</reference> calls to mind <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa 52:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.6">Isa 60:6</reference>; and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.3">Psa 96:3</reference></hi>, Isa 66:19.
entries.5863fd97608ee1d6f0df0f352c175125fb8cbf82: <reference osisRef="Ps.96.4-Ps.96.6">Psa 96:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9946" type="x-p"/> Confirmation of the call from the glory of Jahve that is now become manifest. The clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">Psa 96:4</reference></hi>, as also <reference osisRef="Ps.145.3">Psa 145:3</reference>, is taken out of Psa 48:2. כל־אלהים is the plural of כּל־אלוהּ, every god, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.15">2Ch 32:15</reference>; the article may stand here or be omitted (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.3">Psa 95:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.113.4">Psa 113:4</reference>). All the elohim, i.e., gods, of the peoples are אלילים (from the negative אל), nothings and good-for-nothings, unreal and useless. The lxx renders δαιμόνια, as though the expression were שׁדים (cf. <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.20">1Co 10:20</reference>), more correctly εἴδωλα in Rev 9:20. What <reference osisRef="Ps.96.5">Psa 96:5</reference> says is wrought out in Isa 40, Isa 44, and elsewhere; אלילים is a name of idols that occurs nowhere more frequently than in Isaiah. The sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.6">Psa 96:6</reference>) is here the earthly sanctuary. From Jerusalem, over which the light arises first of all (Isa. 60), Jahve’s superterrestrial doxa now reveals itself in the world. הוד־והדר is the usual pair of words for royal glory. The chronicler reads <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.6">Psa 96:6</reference></hi> עז וחדוה בּמקמו, might and joy are in His place (הדוה( ecalp siH ni era yoj d a late word, like אחוה, brotherhood, brotherly affection, from an old root, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.9">Exo 18:9</reference>). With the place of God one might associate the thought of the celestial place of God transcending space; the chronicler may, however, have altered במקדשׁו into במקמו because when the Ark was brought in, the Temple (בית המקדשׁ) was not yet built.
entries.cf3151fa13ebc8c6ec2160f97ddd259d4d9ad793: <reference osisRef="Ps.96.7-Ps.96.9">Psa 96:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen9946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9947" type="x-p"/> Call to the families of the peoples to worship God, the One, living, and glorious God. הבוּ is repeated three times here as <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference>, of which the whole strophe is an echo. Isaiah (ch. 60) sees them coming in with the gifts which they are admonished to bring with them into the courts of Jahve (in Chr. only: לפניו). Instead of בּהדרת קדשׁ here and in the chronicler, the lxx brings the courts (חצרת) in once more; but the dependence of the strophe upon <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> furnishes a guarantee for the “holy attire,” similar to the wedding garment in the New Testament parable. Instead of מפּניו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.9">Psa 96:9</reference></hi>, the chronicler has מלּפניו, just as he also alternates with both forms, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.7">2Ch 32:7</reference>, cf. 1Ch 19:18.
entries.13f118e17c0b1432ba525be8e8680f1b0f0900f5: <reference osisRef="Ps.96.10-Ps.96.11">Psa 96:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen9947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9948" type="x-p"/> That which is to be said among the peoples is the joyous evangel of the kingdom of heaven which is now come and realized. The watchword is “Jahve is King,” as in Isa 52:7. The lxx correctly renders: ὁ κύριος ἐβασίλευσε<note placement="foot">In the <hi type="italic">Psalterium Veronense</hi> with the addition <hi type="italic">apo xylu,</hi> Cod. 156, Latinizing ἀπὸ τῷ ξύλῳ; in the Latin Psalters (the Vulgate excepted) <hi type="italic">a ligno</hi>, undoubtedly an addition by an early Christian hand, upon which, however, great value is set by Justin and all the early Latin Fathers.</note> for מלך is intended historically (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.17">Rev 11:17</reference>). אף, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>, introduces that which results from this fact, and therefore to a certain extent goes beyond it. The world below, hitherto shaken by war and anarchy, now stands upon foundations that cannot be shaken in time to come, under Jahve’s righteous and gentle sway. This is the joyful tidings of the new era which the poet predicts from out of his own times, when he depicts the joy that will then pervade the whole creation; in connection with which it is hardly intentional that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference></hi> acrostically contain the divine names יהוה and יהו. This joining of all creatures in the joy at Jahve’s appearing is a characteristic feature of Isa 40:1. These cords are already struck in Isa 35:1. “The sea and its fulness” as in Isa 42:10. In the chronicler <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference></hi> (ויאמרו instead of אמרו) stands between <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference></hi> - according to Hitzig, who uses all his ingenuity here in favour of that other recension of the text, by an oversight of the copyist.
entries.f21ea2df38c8b8006026cfc57cb17accd919fc8d: <reference osisRef="Ps.96.12-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen9948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9949" type="x-p"/> The chronicler changes שׂדי into the prosaic השּׂדה, and כל־עצי־יעל with the omission of the כל into עצי היּער. The psalmist on his part follows the model of Isaiah, who makes the trees of the wood exult and clap their hands, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.12">Psa 55:12</reference>; Psa 44:23. The אז, which points into this festive time of all creatures which begins with Jahve’s coming, is as in Isa 35:5. Instead of לפני, “before,” the chronicler has the מלּפני so familiar to him, by which the joy is denoted as being occasioned by Jahve’s appearing. The lines <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Psa 96:13</reference></hi> sound very much like Psa 9:9. The chronicler has abridged <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Psa 96:13</reference>, by hurrying on to the mosaic-work portion taken from Ps 105. The poet at the close glances from the ideal past into the future. The twofold בּא is a participle, Ew. §200. Being come to judgment, after He has judged and sifted, executing punishment, Jahve will govern in the righteousness of mercy and in faithfulness to the promises.  <chapter eID="Ps.96"/> <div eID="gen9949" type="x-p"/>

entries.3390384a89bbaaafca0d455e045b420dd7c7c935:
PSALM 96
This psalm contains an exhortation to praise God, an exhortation which is directed not only to the Jews, but to all nations. We must infer from this, that it has reference to the kingdom of Christ. God’s name could not be called upon in any other part of the world than Judea, until it had been revealed; and the heathen nations were at that time necessarily altogether incapacitated for any such exercise.
“Mutae erant ac surdae.” — Lat.
Yet it is evident that the Holy Spirit stirred up the saints who were under the Law to celebrate the Divine praises, till the period should arrive when Christ, by the spread of the Gospel, should fill the whole earth with his glory.
Psalm 96:1-3
1. Sing to Jehovah a new song, sing unto Jehovah, all the earth. 2. Sing unto Jehovah, bless his name; show forth his salvation from day to day. 3. Declare his glory among the heathen; his wonders among all people.
 
1 Sing unto Jehovah a new song This commencement shows that, as I have already observed, the Psalmist is exhorting the whole world, and not the Israelites merely, to the exercise of devotion. Nor could this be done, unless the gospel were universally diffused as the means of conveying the knowledge of God. The saying of Paul must necessarily hold true,
“How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10:14.)
The same Apostle proves the calling of the Gentiles, by adducing in testimony of it, “Praise the Lord, ye Gentiles, with his people” — from which it follows, that fellowship in the faith stands connected with the joint celebration of praise, (Romans 15:11.) Besides, the Psalmist requires a new song,
We meet with a psalm very similar to this, in 1 Chronicles 16, delivered by David to Asaph, to be sung on occasion of the removing of the ark from the house of Obed-edom to Zion. But the ode, as it stands in 1 Chronicles 16, is considerably longer, extending from the 8th verse to the 36th [1Ch 16:8-36]; and this is only the part of it from the 23rd to the 33rd verse [1Ch 16:23-33]. It has been supposed that this part was extracted from the psalm above mentioned, and, with a few inconsiderable alterations, adapted to the solemnity of the dedication of the second temple. This opinion is founded upon the inscription of the psalm in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Æthiopic, and Arabic versions, which is, “A song of David when the house was built after the captivity.” Consequently, strictly speaking, this is not a new song. But it may be called new, from its having been adapted to a new purpose — from its having been intended to celebrate new mercies conferred upon the Jews, and to lead the mind forward to the glorious era of the coming of the Messiah, and the establishment of his kingdom, which probably was the matter of more general expectation among the chosen people, at the period when the temple was rebuilt, than when the ark was brought to Mount Zion from the house of Obed-edom. It may be observed, that the first verse is not in the original poem, as recorded in the book of Chronicles, but appears to have been added for the new occasion to which this shorter psalm was adapted.
not one which was common, and had formerly been raised. He must therefore refer to some unusual and extraordinary display of the Divine goodness. Thus, when Isaiah speaks of the restoration of the Church, which was wonderful and incredible, he says, “Sing unto the Lord a new song,” (Isaiah 42:10.) The Psalmist intimates accordingly, that the time was come when God would erect his kingdom in the world in a manner altogether unlooked for. He intimates still more clearly as he proceeds, that all nations would share in the favor of God. He calls upon them everywhere to show forth his salvation, and, in desiring that they should celebrate it from day to day, would denote that it was not of a fading or evanescent nature, but such as should endure for ever.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="96" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. XCVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm was composed by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> upon occasion, or at the time, of the bringing of the Ark of God into the Taberna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cle which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had prepared for it in <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> as may be gathered by comparing it with 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16. 7. 23, 24<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> where almost the whole Psalm is to be found. But as the Ark was an evident type of the Messiah, which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> very well knew, as hath been oft noted before; so <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> thoughts, or at least the design of Gods spirit, which indi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted this Psalm, was extended beyond and above it, even to the times of the Messiah, and to his glorious and univer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sal Kingdom, in which not the Jews onely but the Heathen Nations also should worship the true God and kiss his Son the Messiah.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 O <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Chron. 16. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 33. 3.</ns0:note> Sing unto the LORD a new Song <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Upon this new and great occasion, not the removal of the Ark, wherein there was nothing new but an inconsider<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able circumstance of place, and that not yet fixed; but the coming of the Messiah, and the confirming of the New Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant by his blood, and the calling of the Gentiles.</ns0:note>: sing unto the LORD all the earth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">All the Nations of the Earth, who shall then partake of those great blessings and priviledges which are now peculiar to <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Sing unto the LORD, bless his name: shew forth his salvation <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That great work of the redemption and salvation of the World by the Messias.</ns0:note> from day to day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">You who shall be called out of all the Heathen Nations to the knowledge of God and Christ publish this glorious and wonderful work amongst all the Heathen Nations to whom you belong or may come.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 For the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> great, and greatly to be praised: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 95 3.</ns0:note> he is to be feared above all gods <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The gods of the nations as the next Verse ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounds it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For all the gods of the nations <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> idols <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>nothings,</ns0:hi> as they are called, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8. 4. and 10. 19. or <ns0:hi>vain things,</ns0:hi> as the word signifies and is translated by o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers. The sence is, Though they have usurped the name and place of the Divine Majesty, yet they have nothing of his nature or power in them.</ns0:note>; but the LORD made the heavens.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Honour and majesty <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> before him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In his presence, like beams shot out from his face, who is the Sun of righteousness. There is an unconceivable glory and majesty in his countenance and in the place of his presence.</ns0:note>: strength and beauty <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> in his sanctuary <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in his holy place,</ns0:hi> where he records his name and affords his presence. There are the manifestations of Gods power and grace, or goodness, and all his per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Give unto the LORD, O ye kindreds of the people <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>O ye families of the people</ns0:hi> of the World. And the word <ns0:hi>families</ns0:hi> may be understood either 1. strictly and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly; and so it may be intimated that this great blessing of salvation by Christ should not be imparted to whole Nations, but onely to some persons taken <ns0:hi>out of every people and nation,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 5. 9. or 2. more largely for nations, as it is taken <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12. 3. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 25. 9. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 14. 18. and so it may be implied that not onely some few of the Heathen peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple should be brought to the acknowledgment and worship of the true God, as was usual in the times of the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, but that whole Nations should come in to the Church of God together.</ns0:note>: give unto the LORD <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Ascribe to him or acknowledge to be in him.</ns0:note> glory and strength.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 29. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, 2.</ns0:note> Give unto the LORD the glory <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> of his name.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>due unto</ns0:hi> his name: bring an offering and come in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to his courts <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Into the Courts of his House. But under this one part of worship he comprehends the whole of worship of God; and he speaks of the worship of the New Testament under the expressions of legal worship, as the Prophets elsewhere do, as <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 1. 11. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 O worship the LORD <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 110. 3.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> in the glorious sanctu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ary.</ns0:note> in the beauty of holiness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either in the holy place which he shall appoint to that end: or, clothed with all those holy Ornaments, those gifts and graces, which are necessary and required in Gods worship.</ns0:note>: fear before him all the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Say among the heathen <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">You converted Gentiles declare this to those who yet remain in the darkness of Heathenism.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 93. 1. & 97. 1.</ns0:note> the LORD reigneth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That God hath now set up his Throne and Kingdom in the World.</ns0:note>: the world also shall be esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished that it shall not be moved <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And as that <ns0:hi>Kingdom shall never be destroyed</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>shall stand for ever,</ns0:hi> as is said <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 44. so the Nations of the World shall by the means of it enjoy an established and lasting peace; which is every where mentioned as one of the blessings which the Mes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siah shall give to the World, as <ns0:hi>Psal<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> 72. 3, 7. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 9. 6, 7. and 66. 12. <ns0:hi>Mi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 5. 5. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 9. 10.</ns0:note>: he shall judge the people righteously <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He shall not abuse his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vincible power and established dominion to the oppression of his people, as other Princes frequently do, but shall govern them by the rules of justice and equity, which is the onely foundation of a true and solid peace. See <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 32. 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Let the heavens rejoyce, and let the earth be glad <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">It is a figure called <ns0:hi>Prosopopoeia,</ns0:hi> whereby he signifies the great felicity of those times, which shall be such that even those liveless Creatures would testify their joy and thankful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness for it, if they were in a capacity so to do.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 98. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
